questions.q: Why does this lesson say apologizing for the LedgerPoint batch design is a weaker move than defending it as deliberate?
options: Because apologizing invites the board to treat it as an unresolved weakness rather than a deliberate, defensible choice, even though the underlying design is identical either way
Because apologizing is always factually incorrect
Because the LedgerPoint design was actually a mistake that should be apologized for
Because board members prefer long, detailed apologies
questions.explain: Framing changes how the same design gets evaluated — presenting the batch design as a deliberate, engineered answer to a real constraint holds up to scrutiny better than framing it as something the team settled for.

questions.q: In the hostile follow-up mock question ('isn't that just avoiding the hard problem'), what makes the strong answer effective?
options: It concedes the board member is right and apologizes for the design
It changes the subject to a different design area entirely
It stays calm, restates the actual reasoning, and explicitly frames the decision as right for now without claiming it's permanent truth
It argues the board member has no right to ask the question
questions.explain: The strong answer doesn't get rattled by pointed framing — it calmly restates the real reasoning and acknowledges scope (right for now, revisited if circumstances change) without conceding the design was wrong.

questions.q: What would happen to ownership and sharing-recalculation cost if the Meridian integration user, rather than queues, owned every synced Parts Order record?
options: Nothing would change, since ownership doesn't affect sharing calculations
That one user would own tens of millions of records, a severe case of ownership skew, making sharing-recalculation and visibility checks dramatically more expensive
Parts Order would automatically move to a Big Object
The Private OWD would automatically change to Public Read Only
questions.explain: The mock answer walks through the specific consequence: one user owning tens of millions of records creates severe ownership skew, which is exactly what queue-based ownership (Lesson 10) was designed to avoid.

questions.q: What does 'cross-answer consistency' mean, per this lesson?
options: Giving the exact same answer to every question regardless of what's asked
Using identical wording across all deliverables
Agreeing with every point a board member raises
Whether an architect's answers to different questions remain factually consistent with each other across an entire defense session
questions.explain: The lesson defines cross-answer consistency as whether separate answers (e.g., about LedgerPoint and about data architecture) stay factually aligned with each other — a board catches contradictions across a session, not just within a single answer.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say consistency across answers isn't an accident in this capstone's defense preparation?
options: Because the same underlying facts (the ADRs and the scenario's established design decisions) are used throughout, which naturally produces consistent answers
Because the architect memorizes a single fixed script word for word
Because board members never ask about the same topic twice
Because consistency is irrelevant to how a board evaluates a defense
questions.explain: Consistency emerges from grounding every answer in the same previously-established facts (ADRs, the data-ownership map, etc.) rather than improvising a new justification each time a related question comes up.
